## Functions

### `captureRealmLifecycleSessionObservationSource(...args)`

Kernel-private lookup of one original issued session. The native signal synchronously invalidates observation on retirement, disposal, root abort or operator revocation. It is not a retirement receipt or resource-cleanup proof. The original assertCurrent still requires exactly frozen { signal } carrying the original work root. Historical lookup grants no renewed currentness.

### `async createRealmLifecycleSessionAuthority(options)`

Issue one process-local lifecycle authority from a NEW durable reservation. Exact options: { operatorContext, generationStorageView, appId, workSignal, teardownSignal }. Both native signals must be distinct and live; the captured real OperatorContext must match the genuine protected generation-service view. All asynchronous construction steps are fenced against both signals and the captured operator. Failure after a committed reservation consumes a gap and publishes no session. This factory never adopts an observed high-water value. Returned methods consume exact frozen requests. assertCurrent({ signal }) uses the prebound work root. observeRetirement({ signal }) and the authentic single-method retirementHandle.retire({ reason, signal }) use the separately prebound teardown root, including after work abort/operator switch/dispose. Copies, proxies, and unbound extraction of retire are not authentic receivers. dispose() is idempotent listener cleanup and work invalidation, not retirement. Signal abort/operator revocation/retirement also detach all owned listeners. A newer same-account/app reservation does not revoke an older live session. The receipt hashes the bounded canonical eight-field terminal record using SHA-256, prepared privately before issue and exposed only after synchronous retirement. Neither its digest nor the counter is a proof of resource cleanup, durable terminal persistence, previous-process retirement, or pin release. A restarted host must allocate anew; it cannot reconstruct old capabilities or terminal observations from the counter. No old-account I/O is authorized. This is a trusted Kernel construction primitive, NOT lifecyclePort@1 or its process-owner/participant implementation. The separate versioned host-attempt binding captures Entry's roots without widening the existing allocation wire; consuming them in a genuine complete lifecycle port remains integration work. No provider/boot registration, account acquisition grant, origin isolation, runtime activation, or frozen schema/dependency catalog change is introduced.

## Notes & Examples

### Command Bus Pattern

The OS uses a capability-gated command bus for inter-app and system communication. Apps register command handlers; the kernel routes commands based on capabilities. Commands can be local (same app), cross-app (with permission), or system-level (elevated).

**Example: Command registration and invocation**
```js
import { CommandBus } from 'webgpu-os/kernel/CommandBus.js';
import { Capability } from 'webgpu-os/kernel/Capability.js';

const bus = new CommandBus();

// Register a handler (requires 'ui' capability)
bus.register('myapp:openFile', async (path) => {
  const content = await storage.read(path);
  return { content, size: content.length };
}, { capability: 'storage' });

// Invoke locally
const result = await bus.invoke('myapp:openFile', '/docs/readme.md');

// Cross-app invocation (requires 'interop' capability)
const otherApp = bus.proxy('otherapp');
const data = await otherApp.invoke('otherapp:compute', input);

// Broadcast to all listening apps
bus.broadcast('system:themeChanged', { theme: 'dark' });
```

**See also:** [WebGPU OS Architecture](/webgpu-os/architecture.md) · [Security Model](/concepts/security-model.md)
